notes:
Here are my notes on Psalm 104, verse by verse. A few things to know first:

- **Missing sources.** I didn't get to read Pulpit, preceptaustin, the NET Bible notes, or any Catholic, Lutheran or Pentecostal-specific page on this psalm. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching about it, so those are left out.
- **Coverage.** The Ellicott page cut off after v. 15, so his notes stop there.
- **Tradition labels.** Studylight tags Gill as Baptist, Barnes as Presbyterian and Clarke as Wesleyan/Methodist. The Calvin note on v. 15 appears on the same page. Enduring Word is by Pastor David Guzik.

---

**Introduction (whole psalm)**
- **Psalms 103 and 104 as a pair.** Utley says the two form a pair: 103 is about God's covenant love as Redeemer, 104 about God as Creator. Matthew Henry: "God is there praised as the God of grace, here as the God of nature." (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-104; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_104.cfm)
- **Link to Genesis 1.** Guzik says the psalm follows the order of Genesis 1 closely enough to show the writer had the creation account in mind. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-104/)
- **Ellicott's overall view.** He sees the whole hymn as about God's close, continuing relationship with everything He made: God not only started the universe but lives in it and keeps it going. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/104.htm)
- **Who wrote it and when (views differ).**
  - Ellicott says the Hebrew gives no author, while the Greek Old Testament (LXX) names David. He thinks the link with Psalm 103 and an Aramaic word in v. 12 point to a date after the exile. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/104.htm)
  - A Bible Hub article instead supports a date under David, around 1000 BC. (https://biblehub.com/q/What_history_shaped_Psalm_104_s_writing_3.htm)
- **Modern scholarship: the Egyptian hymn.** Bible Odyssey says Psalm 104 "shares a number of motifs with the Great Hymn to the Aten" from Egypt's Amarna period. It is one of only three biblical texts with direct literary parallels to Egyptian writings, though Egyptian influence on the Bible overall is "remarkably low." (https://wwww.bibleodyssey.org/articles/egyptian-influences-on-the-biblical-text/)
  - Utley says the shared features may be deliberate, but there are also clear differences. (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-104)
  - Bible Hub reads the borrowing as a deliberate argument against pagan nature-gods: where pagans worshipped nature, the psalmist shows nature depending completely on the LORD. (https://biblehub.com/q/What_history_shaped_Psalm_104_s_writing_3.htm)
- **Orthodox use in worship.** The Orthodox Church opens Vespers with this psalm (numbered 103 in the Greek Bible). OCA calls it "man's very first act of worship, for man first of all meets God as Creator." (https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/worship/the-daily-cycles-of-prayer/vespers) Singing it recalls the Spirit moving over the waters at creation (Genesis 1), and the opened doors show that humans were first meant to live in Paradise. (https://www.oca.org/cdn/PDFs/evangelization/pamphlets/great-vespers-c.pdf)

---

**v. 1**
- **The psalm's frame.** Psalms 103 and 104 both open and close with "Bless the LORD." Utley calls this praise from humanity, the highest of God's creatures. (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-104)
- **Clothed in majesty.** Ellicott compares Psalm 93:1. Guzik quotes Maclaren: "The Universe is the garment of God." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/104.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-104/)
- **"My God."** Henry says it is the joy of believers that their God is a great God. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_104.cfm)

**v. 2**
- **Light as God's robe.** Ellicott says the psalmist pictures light not as made once and finished but as God's ongoing work: the robe God is always weaving for Himself. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/104.htm)
- **The tent.** The Hebrew word for "curtain" suggests a tent's moving folds. Some see a reference to the Tabernacle curtains, but Ellicott sees no need to limit the picture. (Same URL)
- **Light in this verse.** Utley points out that it describes God Himself, not the dark, formless earth of Genesis 1. (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-104)
- **The stretched-out sky.** Utley calls it a metaphor for the sky's vault. (Same URL)

**v. 3**
- **Beams and chambers.** Ellicott says "lays the beams" is a building term and "chambers" means upper rooms. God's pavilion rests on a floor of rain clouds. The cloud-chariot probably comes from Psalm 18:10. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/104.htm)
- **Not literal.** Utley stresses the picture is unclear and not meant literally. He links it to John Walton's reading of creation as God building His cosmic temple. Clouds are deity's traditional transport and recall the Shekinah cloud of the Exodus. (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-104)
- **Above creation's limits.** Guzik: God is not bound by creation's limits. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-104/)

**v. 4: winds, or angels?** (a real difference in interpretation)
- **Natural forces (Ellicott).** In context the verse means God uses the winds as messengers and lightning as servants. He admits the word order, read alone, favours how Hebrews 1:7 reads it, which was also the traditional Jewish reading. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/104.htm)
- **Natural forces (Utley).** The Hebrew seems to describe nature, not angels. The Greek translation (LXX), which Hebrews 1:7 quotes, turns these forces into servants. (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-104)
- **Angels and Christ (Guzik).** He follows Hebrews: "His" refers to the Messiah, so the angels belong to Jesus, which "confirms the deity of Jesus the Messiah." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-104/)
- **Both (VanGemeren).** Quoted by Guzik: the Lord's servants may be created angels or forces of nature. (Same URL)

**v. 5**
- **Foundations.** Ellicott says the "foundations" here and Job 26:7 (the earth hung "on nothing") are both poetry, not science. He notes the Inquisition used this verse against Galileo. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/104.htm)
- **Built well.** Guzik: what God built He built well, and it stays until He moves it. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-104/)
- **Henry.** The earth stands firm until it gives way to the new earth at the end of time. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_104.cfm)
- **Utley.** The earth often stands for stability, though Psalm 102 speaks of the world passing away. (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-104)

**vv. 6–9: creation or Noah's flood?** (commentators differ)
- **Creation.** Ellicott takes vv. 5–18 as the third day of creation. He notes the psalm has no chaos: mountains and valleys already exist under the sea. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/104.htm)
- **The Flood.** Guzik heads vv. 5–9 as God's power at the Flood and afterwards. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-104/)
- **Henry on v. 9.** The waters covered the earth once, in Noah's day, but never since, because God promised not to drown the world again. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_104.cfm)
- **Bible Hub.** It hears an echo of the Flood in God's set limits. (https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/104.htm)

**v. 7**
- **The water.** Utley notes water is the one thing Genesis 1 doesn't say God spoke into existence. This section, like v. 3, shows His control over it. (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-104)

**v. 8**
- **Hills rise, valleys sink.** Ellicott treats the clause as a parenthesis: mountains rise and valleys sink, which he calls an interesting anticipation of geology. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/104.htm)

**v. 9**
- **The coastline.** For Israel, Ellicott says, the coast was simply God's defence against hostile seas. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/104.htm)
- **Ugarit.** Bible Hub says this counters Canaanite myths of Baal controlling the waters. (https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/104.htm)

**vv. 10–11**
- **Springs first.** Ellicott says the poet thinks first of springs, the wadis or stream valleys that make life possible. He compares the wild donkeys with Job 39:5–8. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/104.htm)
- **Guzik.** After the Flood, God spreads water across the land for every animal. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-104/)

**v. 12**
- **The birds.** Ellicott: they nest in the trees above the streams. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/104.htm)
- **Which birds.** Spurgeon's *Treasury* quotes Canon Tristram, who thought of the bulbul and the nightingale in the Jordan valley. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps104.cfm)

**v. 13**
- **"His works."** Ellicott says the chambers are clouds. "His works" may mean the rain, or nature's fruit-producing work more broadly. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/104.htm)
- **Henry.** "The earth knows when it has enough; it is a pity that any man should not." (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_104.cfm)

**v. 14**
- **"Service" or "labour."** Ellicott says the Hebrew can mean man's "use" or his "labour" of farming. He prefers "use" because of the parallel line. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/104.htm)
- **Guzik.** God designed the world so that with work, people bring food out of the earth. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-104/)
- **Henry.** Our food coming from the earth reminds us we came from the earth and will return to it. We must not live by bread alone. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_104.cfm)

**v. 15: wine** (a point Christians debate; these voices mostly agree)
- **Calvin (Reformed).** Water alone would meet our needs, so wine is a sign of God's extra generosity. Since the psalm doesn't mention excess, it is "lawful to use wine not only in cases of necessity, but also thereby to make us merry." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/104-15.html)
- **Clarke (Wesleyan).** Wine in moderation revives a person. He contrasts it with spirits, which cheer but drain strength. (Same URL)
- **Gill (Baptist).** Wine cheers even the miserable and distressed. (Same URL)
- **Henry.** Wine cheers when used soberly, and it is a pity when it is abused. (Same URL)
- **Got Questions.** It cites the verse to say Scripture warns against misuse of alcohol but does not necessarily forbid drinking. (https://www.gotquestions.org/sin-alcohol.html)
- **Guzik (elsewhere).** "The Bible regards drink, moderately used, as a gift from God (Psalm 104:15)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-28/)
- **Oil and bread.** Ellicott offers "making his face shine more than oil," which Barnes also prefers. "Strengthens" really means "props up," as in "staff of life." Bible Hub links the bread to Christ, the bread of life (John 6:35). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/104.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/104-15.html; https://biblehub.com/psalms/104-15.htm)

**v. 16**
- **Cedars of Lebanon.** Bible Hub notes cedar timbers have been found in palace ruins in Israel, evidence of the trade that supplied Solomon's temple. (https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/104.htm)

**vv. 17–18**
- **Safe homes.** Bible Hub: God gives every creature a safe place to live, even on cedars and crags. (https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/104.htm)

**v. 19**
- **Moon first.** Guzik quotes Maclaren: "The moon is named first, because the Hebrew day began with the evening." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-104/)
- **VanGemeren.** Quoted by Guzik: the Canaanites credited rain, sun and moon to particular gods, but for Israel the Lord rules them all. (Same URL)
- **Henry.** The moon measures the months, guides the farmer's seasons and governs the tides. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_104.cfm)
- **Festival use.** Bible Hub suggests parts may have been sung at the new-moon festival. (https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/104.htm)

**vv. 19–20 (Orthodox)**
- **Evening psalm.** Vespers always opens with this evening psalm. OCA quotes these verses about sunset and night, and grounds the evening start of the church day in Genesis 1:5. (https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/worship/the-daily-cycles-of-prayer/vespers)

**v. 21**
- **Lions seeking food.** Guzik quotes a writer who calls it "a strange expression" that lions should seek their food from God. Neither their strength nor their cunning could feed them without Him. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-104/)

**vv. 22–23**
- **Night and day.** Guzik: when the lions sleep, people go out to work, all following God's wise plan. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-104/)
- **Work and rest.** Bible Hub draws a lesson about balancing them. (https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/104.htm)

**v. 24**
- **Not random.** Guzik: the psalmist sees creation as the wise work of a great God, not the result of random events. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-104/)
- **The Trinity.** Spurgeon's *Treasury* quotes a writer who sees all three persons here. "How many are Your works" points to the Father, and "in wisdom" points to the Son, the eternal Word. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps104.cfm)

**vv. 25–26: Leviathan**
- **Chaos monster tamed.** Bible Hub says Canaanite myths feared Leviathan as a chaos monster. The psalmist removes the terror and shows it simply playing in God's sea. Compare Job 41. (https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/104.htm)
- **Ellicott on the sea.** Israel never delighted in the sea, so here dread turns at most into reverent wonder. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/104.htm)

**v. 27**
- **"In due season."** Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: God gives daily bread proportioned to need. If animals are content with enough, we should not be greedier than they. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-104/)
- **New Testament echoes.** Bible Hub links the verse to Matthew 6:26 and Colossians 1:17. (https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/104.htm)

**v. 28**
- **God gives, we gather.** Guzik (Spanish edition): God provides, but we must gather it; His provision is around us and calls for wisdom and effort. (https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/salmo-104/)

**v. 29**
- **Utter dependence.** Guzik: creation depends on God so completely that it would die if He withdrew. In a real sense creation is more yielded to God than humanity is. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-104/)

**v. 30: the Spirit** (several readings)
- **Breath or Spirit.** The BSB footnote allows "breath" in place of "Spirit." (https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/104.htm)
- **Ongoing creation.** Guzik, via Spurgeon, quotes Caryl: "Providence is creation continued." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-104/)
- **Henry.** The same Spirit that created all things keeps them going, as each generation replaces the last. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_104.cfm)
- **Gill (Baptist).** Following the Targum (the Aramaic paraphrase), he takes it as the Holy Spirit. He applies it to the Spirit renewing souls, to the new state of things at Pentecost, and to a future new heavens and earth. (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/psalms/104-30.html; https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nrs/psalms/104-30.html)
- **Clarke (Wesleyan).** He asks whether it implies a resurrection, mainly of animals, connected with Romans 8:19–23. (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/psalms/104-30.html)
- **Jewish readers.** Gill and Henry both note that some apply it to the resurrection of the dead. (Same URL; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/104-30.html)
- **Bible Hub.** It reads the Spirit as the Holy Spirit and links the verse to new birth, Titus 3:5 and the new creation. (https://biblehub.com/study/psalms/104-30.htm)

**v. 31**
- **Prayer or prediction.** Barnes and Poole say it can be read as a prayer ("Let the glory…") or as a confident statement. The Targum, the Greek and the Latin Vulgate render it as a prayer. Keil and Delitzsch call vv. 31–35 a "sabbatic" (Sabbath-like) close. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/104-31.htm)
- **Spurgeon.** God's works may pass, but not His glory. He will rejoice more fully when the earth is renewed. (Same URL)
- **Guzik.** People, who can choose, should deliberately give God reason to rejoice. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-104/)

**v. 32**
- **Sinai.** Guzik suggests the trembling earth and smoking hills may recall Mount Sinai (Exodus 19). Henry makes the same link. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-104/; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_104.cfm)

**v. 33**
- **"In my lives."** Spurgeon says the Hebrew is literally "in my lives," meaning praise here and hereafter. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps104.cfm)
- **Guzik.** The psalm hardly mentions redemption, yet knowing God as Creator was enough to stir lifelong praise. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-104/)

**v. 34**
- **"Meditation."** Ellicott renders it "my singing" or "my poetry." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/104.htm)
- **Guzik.** God is also worshipped by our thoughts. He quotes Spurgeon that redemption is an even richer subject for meditation than creation. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-104/)

**v. 35: the closing curse** (commentators handle it differently)
- **Ellicott.** He notes this curse in an otherwise glad hymn "has been variously excused." He puts it down to national feeling against heathen oppressors. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/104.htm)
- **Spurgeon's *Treasury*.** It quotes a writer who says the wicked corrupt God's world by abusing His gifts, so the prophet rightly desires their end. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps104.cfm)
- **Guzik.** It follows logically for those who reject God as Creator, but the psalm won't end on a dark note. (https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/salmo-104/)
- **Utley.** It is the "beyond day 7" step, the Fall of Genesis 3. The ending echoes Psalm 103's double "bless." (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-104)
- **"Hallelujah."** The BSB footnote explains it means "Praise the LORD." (https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/104.htm)
